title: Ham Radio and the Hams Who Use Them
summary: Josh and Chuck explore amateur ("ham") radio: its size and demographics, the origin of the name "ham," how shortwave propagation works via the ionosphere, the amateur frequency bands, repeaters, VHF/FM, two-way conversation etiquette and the community's reputation for politeness, QSL cards, Morse code testing (since dropped), talking to astronauts and orbiting ISS-style contacts, rogue/pirate ham operators, licensing tiers and the US test, equipment (transceivers, analog vs digital), improvised antennas, celebrity hams, and getting started through Elmers and clubs. The episode closes with a listener email from a marathon runner named Marco.

entities.name: Ham Radio: Ancestors of the Internet

segments.title: Squarespace and Google sponsor read
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Squarespace and Google business tools, with an offer code.

segments.title: Opening banter on ham radio
segments.summary: Hosts introduce ham radio, also called amateur or shortwave radio, cite operator numbers in the US and abroad, and discuss the hobby's polite, professional reputation and its mostly male demographic.

segments.title: Origin of the word ham
segments.summary: The hosts explain that 'ham' was originally a derogatory term for amateur operators who jammed government and commercial signals, and that operators adopted it with pride. They mention a less credible origin story involving a Harvard radio club.

segments.title: AM bands and the radio spectrum
segments.summary: Hosts describe the AM band and the amateur allocations of twenty-six bands, and explain how the frequencies relate to the spectrum.

segments.title: Ionosphere, shortwave propagation and line of sight
segments.summary: Explanation of how shortwave signals reflect off the ionosphere, allowing long-distance communication, why nighttime propagation is better than daytime, and how VHF and above works line of sight.

segments.title: Repeaters and VHF FM
segments.summary: The hosts discuss repeaters that relay signals from high-power towers over VHF FM and how operators use them.

segments.title: What hams do: listening, QSOs, QSL cards, and etiquette
segments.summary: Operators listen across frequencies and hold two-way conversations, sometimes in nets. QSL cards serve as confirmation postcards. The community's politeness is contrasted with internet chat rooms and CB radio.

segments.title: Morse code and cursive
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the former Morse code licensing test, which has been dropped, and ham purists who still use Morse. They reflect on losing cursive writing.

segments.title: Talking to astronauts
segments.summary: Astronauts are generally ham licensed and can talk to schools and people on Earth via amateur radio, with contacts that previously required being directly overhead.

segments.title: Rogue hams and the pirate ham operator
segments.summary: A pirate operator who ran an unlicensed, ranting broadcast on a shortwave frequency was sued by the government; he countersued for fifty million dollars and the suit was dismissed. The hosts contrast him with the community norm.

segments.title: Ham and food banter
segments.summary: Brief light banter about ham as food, including honey baked ham and processed meats.

segments.title: Licensing, age, Kids Day, and emergency communications
segments.summary: There is no age restriction, licensing is by country, and the US uses a multiple-choice test with three license classes. Kids Day introduces young people to the hobby. The hosts discuss ham radio's use in natural disasters and the appeal of volunteer service.

segments.title: Equipment, transceivers, and analog vs digital radios
segments.summary: Hosts explain the basics of how radio waves are transmitted and received by antennas, and describe transceiver price ranges and analog versus digital tuning. They also discuss sharing frequencies to avoid interference.

segments.title: Improvised antennas and burglar tape
segments.summary: Hams use unusual objects as antennas, including window screens, ladders, rain gutters, slinkies, and wire strung between buildings. Hosts also mention an obscure term, burglar tape, that they could not verify.

segments.title: Getting started, clubs, Elmers, and celebrity hams
segments.summary: Hosts describe ham fests, Elmers as mentors, and the ARRL and an Atlanta club formed in 1911. They list celebrity hams including Ronnie Milsap, Joe Walsh, Gary Shandling, Priscilla Presley, King Hussein, Barry Goldwater, Chet Atkins, and Marlon Brando, and explain the term silent key.

segments.title: Listener mail from Marco
segments.summary: Marco, training for the New York City Marathon, thanks the show for helping him through training and suggests a marathon episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact information and sign off.
